title: Relative marked-anodyne lifting and mapping complexes
statement:
Use marked simplicial sets, products and internal Homs as in [lem-coef-marked-point-cartesian-model], the marked-anodyne class and its small generating set in [lem-coef-marked-anodyne-lifting-calculus], and the horn definitions of [def-coef-infinity-fibrations]. These horn definitions are used for arbitrary small simplicial sets: a cartesian fibration $q:Z\to S$ is an inner fibration with a cartesian lift with prescribed target of every base edge, with cartesian edges defined by the final-horn lifting criterion for $n\geq2$, without assuming $S$ or $Z$ quasicategories. Write $Z^\natural$ for exactly its cartesian edges. A marked object over $S$ is equivalently a marked map to $S^\sharp$. For $\epsilon=\flat,\sharp$ put $\operatorname{Map}^\epsilon_S(U,V)_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{/S}(U\times(\Delta^n)^\epsilon,V)$, with the base map ignoring $\Delta^n$.

For every small simplicial set $S$, a marked map $V\to S^\sharp$ has the right lifting property against every marked-anodyne map if and only if it is $Z^\natural\to S^\sharp$ for a cartesian fibration $Z\to S$. Here a map over $S$ is called marked anodyne when its underlying marked map belongs to the marked-anodyne class; this does not assert stability of that class under pullback. For every marked $U$ over $S$ and cartesian $Z\to S$, $\operatorname{Map}^\flat_S(U,Z^\natural)$ is a quasicategory and $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_S(U,Z^\natural)$ is its core and is Kan. Restriction along any monomorphism $U\hookrightarrow V$ over $S$ is a Kan fibration on these sharp mapping complexes, and is a trivial Kan fibration if the monomorphism is marked anodyne.

For any $a:T\to S$, the pullback of a cartesian fibration is cartesian and its cartesian edges are exactly the edges whose images in $Z$ are cartesian; thus the pulled-back marking is its natural marking. Over a quasicategory $S$, the total space $Z$ is a quasicategory and $q:Z\to S$ is a fibration in the Joyal model structure of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]. All the assertions are universe-relative and require no relative marked model structure as a hypothesis.

source.place: Remark 3.1.1.10; Remark 3.1.3.1; Lemma 3.1.3.6; Proposition 2.4.2.3 (base change); Proposition 2.4.1.5 and Corollary 2.4.6.5 (Joyal fibration over a quasicategory) Read from HTT-second-reading.pdf in the delivery sandbox; no Stacks tag states this simplicial result. Not archived in project literature/.

proof.text: First record the elementary horn reductions used below. For any inner fibration $p:E\to B$, a pullback $E\times_B B'\to B'$ is inner: compose an inner-horn square with $B'\to B$, take its filler in $E$, and pair that filler with the already specified simplex in $B'$. If the image of an edge in $E$ is $p$-cartesian, the same pairing fills every final horn for that edge in the pullback. Thus cartesian edges are preserved by pullback; reflection is not asserted here. The same construction pulls a cartesian lift with prescribed target back along a specified edge of $B'$, proving that a pullback of a cartesian fibration is cartesian. A fiber of an inner fibration is a quasicategory, since an inner horn in it lies over the constant simplex of $B$. If $B$ is a quasicategory, fill the image of an inner horn in $B$ and then lift it, so $E$ is a quasicategory. In particular $E_\beta=E\times_B\Delta^m$ is a quasicategory for every simplex $\beta:\Delta^m\to B$: an inner horn in $\Delta^m=N([m])$ determines a nondecreasing chain of vertices and is filled by that chain. All these statements use the arbitrary-simplicial-set horn definitions, not the quasicategory-only wording of the fibration definition.

We will use a cartesian triangle rule only when both total space and base are quasicategories. For a triangle with consecutive edges $g:x\to x'$, $e':x'\to y$ and long edge $e:x\to y$, if $e'$ is cartesian, then $g$ is cartesian if and only if $e$ is cartesian. To obtain this from [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-composition-initiality], take opposites: the simplex operator $\theta:[a]\to[b]$ becomes $i\mapsto b-\theta(a-i)$, exchanging the $i$th and $(n-i)$th horns. Thus inner fibrations and quasicategories remain so, and final-horn cartesian edges become initial-horn cocartesian edges. The opposite triangle has consecutive edges $(e')^{\mathrm{op}},g^{\mathrm{op}}$, so the cited composition equivalence gives exactly the rule. Also, an equivalence edge of the total quasicategory is cartesian for any inner fibration to a quasicategory: every required final-horn square fills by [lem-cbc-inner-fibration-equivalence-outer-horn-lift]. In particular degenerate edges are cartesian in this quasicategory setting.

source.place: Proposition 2.4.1.7; equivalence-edge lifting in Proposition 2.4.1.5 and Corollary 2.4.1.6, with the former direction supplied by the existing relative outer-horn lemma.

proof.text: Here is the comparison needed for an arbitrary base. Let $p:E\to B$ be inner, let $e:x\to y$ lie over $\alpha:s\to t$, and suppose there is a $p$-cartesian edge $e':x'\to y$ over the same $\alpha$. Call $e$ locally cartesian if $(e,\operatorname{id}_{\Delta^1})$ is cartesian in $E_\alpha\to\Delta^1$. Use the final-horn condition of $e'$ in dimension two, with long edge $e$ and base simplex $s_0\alpha$ (vertices $s,s,t$), to obtain a triangle with consecutive edges $g:x\to x'$, $e'$, and long edge $e$, with $g$ in the fiber $E_s$. If $e$ is locally cartesian, this triangle pulled to $E_\alpha\to\Delta^1$ has both $e,e'$ cartesian. Its total space and base are quasicategories by Step 1. The triangle rule of Step 2 makes $g$ cartesian there. Pull it further to the vertex $0$ of $\Delta^1$: $g$ is cartesian for $E_s\to\Delta^0$. This is exactly the absolute final-outer-horn property, so [lem-cbc-equivalence-outer-horn-filling] makes $g$ an equivalence in $E_s$. This proves the fiber-equivalence claim with its precise fiber, rather than treating equivalence in $E_\alpha$ as equivalence in $E_s$.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 3.1.1.6; Remark 2.4.2.13; comparison triangle and equivalence in the source fiber.

proof.text: Continue with the comparison triangle in Step 3 and its fiber equivalence $g$. Consider any final-horn square for $e$, with base $\beta:\Delta^n\to B$, $n\geq2$. Its final base edge is $\alpha$. In $E_\beta\to\Delta^n$, lift the comparison triangle using the vertex map $[2]\to[n]$ with values $(n-1,n-1,n)$. Its first edge is the image of $g$ under the inclusion of the fiber at $n-1$. That inclusion preserves the two inverse triangles, so this first edge is an equivalence in the quasicategory $E_\beta$. By the relative equivalence outer-horn lemma it is cartesian for $E_\beta\to\Delta^n$. The last edge, coming from $e'$, is cartesian by Step 1. The triangle rule therefore makes the long edge, coming from $e$, cartesian in $E_\beta$. It fills the specified horn, and projection gives a filler in $E$. Since the horn was arbitrary, $e$ is $p$-cartesian. We have proved: local cartesianness plus a global cartesian lift over the same edge with the same target implies global cartesianness. No supply of other cartesian lifts, and no quasicategory hypothesis on $B$, was used.

source.place: Remark 2.4.2.13, with the reduction to each base simplex and the final-horn argument written out.

proof.text: Apply Steps 1 and 4 to a cartesian fibration $q:Z\to S$ and $a:T\to S$. The pullback $q_T:T\times_S Z\to T$ is cartesian by Step 1, and it preserves cartesian edges. Conversely, if an edge $h$ in the pullback is cartesian, pull it to its own base edge $\delta:\Delta^1\to T$. The degreewise identity $(T\times_S Z)\times_T\Delta^1=Z\times_S\Delta^1$, using $a\delta$ on the right, says that its image $e$ in $Z$ is locally $q$-cartesian. Choose a global $q$-cartesian lift of $q(e)$ with target the target of $e$; this uses the defining lift-existence hypothesis for $q$. Step 4 makes $e$ globally cartesian. Thus the cartesian edges of the pullback are exactly those mapping to cartesian edges of $Z$. This proves the reflection direction that a direct pullback-of-fillers argument alone cannot give.

source.place: Proposition 2.4.2.3(2); Remark 2.4.1.12; Remark 2.4.2.13. Elementary application of Steps 1 and 4.

proof.text: The natural marking for a cartesian fibration over an arbitrary $S$ contains all degenerate edges. Indeed, a degenerate edge at $z\in Z_s$ lies over the constant edge at $s$. Over that edge the pullback is $Z_s\times\Delta^1$. Its edge $(\operatorname{id}_z,[0,1])$ is cartesian for projection to $\Delta^1$: project a final-horn square to the quasicategory $Z_s$, fill its horn ending in the equivalence $\operatorname{id}_z$ by [lem-cbc-equivalence-outer-horn-filling], and pair with the prescribed base simplex. Thus the edge is locally cartesian. A global cartesian lift over the same constant edge with target $z$ exists, so Step 4 proves that the original degenerate edge is cartesian. Hence $Z^\natural$ is a marked set. A marked object over $S$ is the same as a marked map to $S^\sharp$, since the latter puts no restriction on images of marked edges.

source.place: Definition 3.1.1.8; arbitrary-base degeneracy check using Remark 2.4.2.13 and the absolute outer-horn criterion.

proof.text: Suppose $p:V\to S^\sharp$ lifts every marked-anodyne map. Family (i) of [lem-coef-marked-anodyne-lifting-calculus] makes the underlying map inner. Family (ii) for $n\geq2$ makes each marked edge cartesian, and its $n=1$ map $\{1\}^\sharp\to(\Delta^1)^\sharp$ supplies a marked cartesian lift of every base edge with prescribed target. Thus the underlying map is a cartesian fibration. To prove that every cartesian edge $e:x\to y$ is marked, choose such a marked cartesian lift $e':x'\to y$ with the same base edge. Step 3 applies (global implies local by Step 1) and gives a triangle $(g,e',e)$ with $g$ an equivalence in $V_s$. By [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus] the core $K=(V_s)^\simeq$ is Kan. Apply the lifting property to $K^\flat\to K^\sharp$ with base map constant at $s$ and upper map the core inclusion into $V$. It forces every edge of $K$, in particular $g$, to be marked. Family (iii), applied to this triangle with its two consecutive edges $g,e'$ already marked, forces $e$ to be marked. Therefore $V$ has exactly its cartesian edges marked.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.1.6, only-if proof; Remark 3.1.1.10. The comparison uses Steps 1 and 3, not an unquoted marking criterion.

proof.text: Conversely let $q:Z\to S$ be cartesian with its natural marking. Family (i) lifts by innerness. Family (ii) lifts by the final-horn definition for $n\geq2$ and by the specified-target cartesian lifts for $n=1$. For family (iii), its base map is a simplex $\Delta^2\to S$. Pull back to this simplex. The total space is a quasicategory by Step 1; Step 5 identifies the pulled-back marking with its cartesian edges. The triangle rule of Step 2 makes the long edge cartesian when the two consecutive edges are cartesian. Step 5 then identifies its image as a marked edge in $Z$, providing the required marking extension. For family (iv), pull back along its arbitrary base map $K\to S$ to $Z_K\to K$. Since $K$ is Kan, it is a quasicategory and every edge is an equivalence by [lem-cbc-equivalence-outer-horn-filling]. The total space $Z_K$ is a quasicategory by Step 1. The given map $K\to Z$ becomes a section $K\to Z_K$; it preserves inverse-triangle witnesses, so every image edge is an equivalence in $Z_K$. The relative outer-horn lemma makes these edges cartesian for $Z_K\to K$, and Step 5 reflects them to cartesian edges of $Z$. This fills the marking extension $K^\flat\to K^\sharp$. The base map $K\to S$ has not been assumed constant.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.1.6, converse proof, including the reductions to Delta^2 and to the arbitrary Kan base K.

proof.text: For a fixed right map, the class of left maps it lifts is closed under the three operations defining marked anodyne maps. A square out of a pushout is solved on the attached map and glued by the pushout property. For a continuous transfinite composite choose successive extensions, and at a limit ordinal take their compatible union by the colimit property. A square on a retract is included in the larger square, filled there and projected by the retraction. Applying this to Step 8 extends its lifting property from the four families to all marked-anodyne maps. Together with Step 7 this proves the relative lifting equivalence.

source.place: Definition 3.1.1.1 and Proposition 3.1.1.6; explicit weak-saturation argument.

proof.text:
Fix $U\to S$ and $q:Z\to S$ cartesian. Form the marked relative internal Hom
$$H=(Z^\natural)^U\times_{(S^\sharp)^U}(\Delta^0)^\sharp,$$
where the point selects the given map $U\to S$. Pullbacks of marked sets have degreewise underlying pullbacks, with an edge marked when each projection is marked; this formula satisfies the universal property by testing edges. By the internal-Hom adjunction in [lem-coef-marked-point-cartesian-model], the underlying simplicial set of $H$ is $\operatorname{Map}^\flat_S(U,Z^\natural)$, and its all-marked-edge simplicial subset is $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_S(U,Z^\natural)$. For any marked-anodyne $i:A\to B$, a square $A\to H$ over the terminal point adjoints to a lifting problem for $q$ against
$$i\square(\varnothing\to U)=i\times U,$$
whose base map is $U\times B\to U\to S$. This left map is marked anodyne by the pushout-product assertion of [lem-coef-marked-anodyne-lifting-calculus], and $q$ lifts it by Step 9. Thus $H\to*$ lifts all marked-anodyne maps. The point recognition statement of that same cited node gives $H=C^\natural$ for a quasicategory $C$. Consequently the relative flat mapping object is a quasicategory, and the relative sharp mapping object is exactly its core and is Kan. This uses the point theorem on the marked set $H$ that has just been shown fibrant, not on $Z$ over a nonterminal base.

source.place: Remark 3.1.3.1; Proposition 3.1.2.3; marked internal-Hom adjunction and the point recognition theorem.

proof.text: For later restriction tests, the fully marked positive-index horns $h_{k,n}:(\Lambda_k^n)^\sharp\to(\Delta^n)^\sharp$, $0<k\leq n$, are marked anodyne. If $n\geq3$, the horn contains every edge; attach its missing simplex using family (i) when $k<n$ or (ii) when $k=n$, retaining all source markings by pushout. For $n=2,k=1$, first fill the minimal inner horn retaining its two marked consecutive edges, and then use family (iii) to mark the long edge. For $n=2,k=2$, first use family (ii), retaining the marked long and final edges; then [lem-coef-marked-triangle-cancellation] marks the remaining first edge. For $n=1,k=1$, the map is family (ii) itself. These constructions give exactly the fully marked codomain, with no claim that every fully marked horn is anodyne.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.3.6, positive sharp-horn attachments; Corollary 3.1.1.7 for the two-dimensional final horn.

proof.text: Let $j:U\hookrightarrow V$ be a marked map over $S$ injective on underlying simplices, and let $r$ be restriction on the sharp mapping objects. A square against a positive-index horn $\Lambda_k^n\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$ for $r$ adjoints to a square for $q:Z^\natural\to S^\sharp$ with left map $j\square h_{k,n}$; its bottom map is induced by $V\to S$ and ignores the simplex coordinate. Step 11 and the pushout-product theorem make this left map marked anodyne, and Step 9 fills it. Thus $r$ is a right fibration. Its target is Kan by Step 10. Applying [lem-cbc-right-fibration-space-fiber] gives all missing index-zero horn lifts, hence $r$ is a Kan fibration. This checks the Kan-base hypothesis of that lemma explicitly.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.3.6 and the right-fibration-over-a-Kan-base theorem (dual of Lemma 2.1.3.3).

proof.text:
If $j$ is marked anodyne, a boundary lifting problem for $r$ adjoints instead to a square for $q$ with left map
$$j\square\bigl((\partial\Delta^n)^\sharp\hookrightarrow(\Delta^n)^\sharp\bigr).$$
The boundary map is degreewise injective, so the pushout-product theorem makes this map marked anodyne. Step 9 fills the square. This holds also for $n=0$, whose boundary is empty, giving extension of a vertex of the mapping object. By the boundary-lifting characterization in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], $r$ is a trivial Kan fibration.

For completeness, derive the cartesian-equivalence fact needed for the Joyal assertion from existing triangle lemmas. Let $p:E\to B$ be an inner fibration between quasicategories and $e:x\to y$ cartesian with $p(e)$ an equivalence. Choose an inverse $v:p(y)\to p(x)$ with both inverse triangles. The final-horn lifting property of $e$ over the triangle with consecutive edges $(v,p(e))$ and long edge $\operatorname{id}_{p(y)}$ gives $r:y\to x$ over $v$ and a triangle $er=\operatorname{id}_y$. The identity of $y$ is cartesian by Step 2. Applying the triangle rule to $(r,e,\operatorname{id}_y)$ makes $r$ cartesian. Use its final-horn property over the other inverse triangle, with consecutive edges $(p(e),v)$ and long edge $\operatorname{id}_{p(x)}$, to get $s:x\to y$ and $rs=\operatorname{id}_x$. In the category $hE$ of [lem-coef-homotopy-category-triangle-calculus], these triangles give $[e][r]=1$ and $[r][s]=1$. Hence $[e]=[e][r][s]=[s]$ and $[r][e]=1$. The same cited lemma realizes the latter equality by a two-simplex with edges $(e,r,\operatorname{id}_x)$. Together with the first triangle this makes $e$ an equivalence. The converse, that an equivalence is cartesian, was supplied by the relative outer-horn lemma in Step 2. This is a proof of the needed fact inside the item, not a new node restating its Joyal clause.

source.place: Proposition 2.4.1.5; proof here by specified inverse triangles, relative final-horn lifts and cartesian cancellation.

proof.text: Now suppose $S$ is a quasicategory. Step 1 makes $Z$ a quasicategory. To check the source-equivalence-lifting criterion of [lem-coef-joyal-quasicategory-characterizations], fix $z\in Z$ and an equivalence $\alpha:q(z)\to t$. Choose an inverse $\beta:t\to q(z)$ and a specified triangle $\beta\alpha=\operatorname{id}_{q(z)}$. Take a cartesian lift $b:w\to z$ over $\beta$ with target $z$. Step 14 makes $b$ an equivalence. Its final-horn property, applied over that specified triangle with long edge $\operatorname{id}_z$ and final edge $b$, gives $a:z\to w$ with $q(a)=\alpha$ and triangle $ba=\operatorname{id}_z$. Since $[b]$ is invertible in $hZ$, this forces $[a]=[b]^{-1}$; the triangle-realization assertion of [lem-coef-homotopy-category-triangle-calculus] gives the two inverse witnesses for $a$. Thus $a$ is an equivalence with the prescribed source and exact base edge. The inner-fibration hypothesis already holds, so characterization (1) of the cited Joyal theorem makes $q$ a Joyal fibration. The argument explicitly converts target-prescribed cartesian lifts into source-prescribed equivalence lifts.

source.place: Proposition 2.4.1.5; Corollary 2.4.6.5; the existing Joyal quasicategory fibration characterization (1).

proof.text: Every step is performed in the input universe. Fibers and pullbacks are degreewise subsets of products of small sets; marked internal Homs have degrees subsets of sets of maps between fixed small simplicial sets. The cores used in Step 7 are simplicial subsets of small fibers. All horn and boundary domains are finite; the Kan-complex generators can be replaced by the small set of countable Kan complexes supplied by [lem-coef-marked-anodyne-lifting-calculus]. The transfinite extension argument of Step 9 is along the small chains in the definition of weak saturation, not a construction indexed by all objects over $S$. The chosen inverse edges, triangles and fillers stay in the sets already under discussion. Thus none of the arguments uses a relative marked model structure or a universe beyond the stated conventions, and the assertions hold in each such universe.

source.place: Remark 3.1.1.3; universe bookkeeping for the relative marked internal Hom and horn arguments above.
